untested: Whether coastal sea-salt deposition raises soil sodium and weakens aggregates. No paper matched this wording.

web.text: Coastal soils do show more exchangeable sodium close to the coast, with soils nearest the shore past saline-sodic limits and 1.5-2 km inland not. One Egyptian transect showed no steady trend. No source measured aggregate stability, so the aggregate-weakening step is untested.

why: The sodium rise near coasts is known; the aggregate-stability part is new but expected.

untested: Whether soil Streptomyces aerosols seed cloud droplets or ice. Four papers matched but all are unrelated (enzyme expression, indoor spore release).

web.text: Raindrops are known to throw soil bacteria into the air, and fungal spores can act as ice nuclei. Nothing found on Streptomyces or geosmin particles acting as cloud nuclei.

why: Spores are rare cloud nuclei and no evidence points to Streptomyces or geosmin.

untested: Phage killing of methane-oxidizing bacteria and its effect on methane oxidation.

papers.title: T4-type phages diversity in wetland soils reveals their ubiquity and their likely host-dependent dynamics

web.text: No soil study shows phage lysis lowering methane uptake. A bioreactor report says phage blooms can set back methane oxidizers, supporting the direction. A lake study found phages that carry a methane-oxidation gene, which hints at the opposite effect. Sediment work found viruses infect methanotrophs but their genes do not directly drive methane metabolism.

why: No soil data; evidence for and against the direction.

untested: Soil respiration response to aerosol-scattered light. The matched paper models carbon fluxes in smoke haze.

papers.title: Modeling the radiative effects of biomass burning aerosols on carbon fluxes in the Amazon region

web.text: Smoke haze with moderate aerosol raised canopy photosynthesis, which supports the first step. Nobody has measured the root or soil respiration response. A 2025 preprint calls the root-respiration link largely theoretical. Near volcanoes, geological CO2 can be mistaken for soil respiration.

why: Diffuse light does raise photosynthesis; a root-respiration response is plausible but hard to separate from temperature.

untested: Shifts in nematode life-history groups by ash thickness.

papers.title: Litter microbial and soil faunal communities stimulated in the wake of a volcanic eruption in a semi‐arid woodland in Patagonia, Argentina
Influence of volcanic ash on infectivity and reproduction of two species of meloidogyne

web.text: After the 2011 Puyehue-Cordon Caulle ash fall in Patagonia, nematode numbers and soil enzyme activity dropped. That study did not report life-history (c-p) groups, so the claim about which nematodes go first is untested.

why: Fits known nematode ecology, so likely true, but part of it is expected from existing theory.

untested: Whether protist and earthworm silicon pools lower catchment silica export.

papers.title: Phytolith transport in soil: a laboratory study on intact soil cores
The ultrastructure of Heleopera petricola an agglutinate soil amoeba; with comments on feeding and silica deposition

web.text: Silica-shelled soil amoebae make a silicon pool about half the size of tree uptake in a beech forest, and stream silica exports were too high for rock weathering alone. That suggests biological pools feed silica exports, possibly the opposite of this prediction. Nothing found on earthworms.

why: Evidence may point the opposite way, and the earthworm part is untested.

untested: Whether real lightning strikes raise gene transfer in the field. The lab step is shown.

papers.title: Isolation of lightning-competent soil bacteria

web.text: Lab-scale lightning moved genes into bacteria in soil, and lightning-competent soil bacteria were isolated. One estimate puts the affected soil at 2 to 950 cubic metres per strike. Natural field transfer has not been shown, and no study looked at microbes in fulgurites or strike zones.

links.label: Lab lightning gene transfer in soil

why: Lab mechanism is shown; detecting it at real strike sites is hard.

untested: Coastal field effects and the loss of bioturbation and litter breakdown. Survival and reproduction are tested in the lab.

papers.title: Effects of NaCl and seawater induced salinity on survival and reproduction of three soil invertebrate species

web.text: Mesocosm work shows enchytraeids drop at once under seawater intrusion, with delayed effects on earthworms and plants. Lab tests show salinity cuts survival and reproduction of standard soil invertebrates, including springtails. Bioturbation and litter breakdown in coastal soils were not measured.

links.label: Seawater and NaCl on soil invertebrates

why: Most of the fauna effect is already shown; the bioturbation consequence is the new part.

untested: Upland soils with high-affinity methane oxidizers. Grazing is shown in rice soil.

papers.title: Selective grazing of methanotrophs by protozoa in a rice field soil
A methane-driven microbial food web in a wetland rice soil

web.text: No study of protist grazing on upland methane oxidizers. Upland methane uptake is mostly explained by soil moisture and diffusion, and grazing does not appear in that work.

why: Grazing of methane oxidizers is shown in rice soil, upland is untested, and slow-growing upland oxidizers may be limited by other things.

untested: Springtail gut N2O emission and the antibiotic test.

papers.title: Influence of Lumbricus terrestris and Folsomia candida on N2 O formation pathways in two different soils - with particular focus on N2 emiss
Exploring the relationships between soil fauna, different tillage regimes and CO2 and N2O emissions from black soil in China

web.text: No direct measurement of springtail N2O. Earthworm guts emit N2O, and antibiotics cut earthworm emission by 80%, which points to gut bacteria. Aquatic invertebrates emit N2O from anoxic guts. The Folsomia gut is dense with bacteria.

why: Springtail guts are anoxic and bacteria-rich like earthworm guts, but nobody has measured it.

untested: Termites, and mineral dissolution per unit rock in the field.

papers.title: [Effects of adding basalt powder on organic carbon sequestration in red and yellow-brown soils under earthworm inoculation]

web.text: Earthworms amplified basalt weathering signals (pH, alkalinity, calcium, magnesium, silicon) in mesocosms, and ants broke down silicate minerals 50 to 300 times faster in a burial study. Net CO2 drawdown is unclear because worms also speed organic matter decomposition. No termite study.

why: Largely shown for earthworms and ants already.

untested: Whether burial depth and acidification predict loss of diversity.

papers.title: Soil microbial community composition and co-occurrence network responses to mild and severe disturbances in volcanic areas

web.text: Chronosequences show soil communities shift with age after eruptions, and acidophilic iron oxidizers pioneer fresh deposits. No study compared diversity before and after burial, so the severity-diversity link is untested.

links.label: Soils of different ages after eruptions

why: Community shifts are known; the severity-diversity gradient is untested.

untested: Earlier rain or snow over the dust source. Ice nucleation by soil dust is studied.

papers.title: The relevance of nanoscale biological fragments for ice nucleation in clouds
Ice nucleation ability of loess from the northwestern United States

web.text: Organic-rich agricultural soil dust nucleates ice about as well as desert dust, and organic particles dominate above -36 C. Nothing found on earlier rain or snow over the dust source region.

links.label: Organic matter and ice nuclei of agricultural soil

why: Ice nucleation is established; a measurable rain effect over the source is unlikely to be detectable.

untested: Soil type and land management effects on cloud glaciation downwind.

papers.title: The relevance of nanoscale biological fragments for ice nucleation in clouds
Ice nucleation ability of loess from the northwestern United States

web.text: Soil dust with organic matter nucleates ice at warmer temperatures than mineral dust, and arable emissions peak at harvest. Climate models do not separate soil dust from mineral dust, and no study quantified how land management changes cloud glaciation.

links.label: Organic matter and ice nuclei of agricultural soil

why: The ice-nucleation part is established; the downstream effect is hard to test.

untested: Years-long differences in the methane sink after fire.

papers.title: Methanotrophic bacteria in boreal forest soil after fire
Thinning reduces soil carbon dioxide but not methane flux from southwestern USA ponderosa pine forests

web.text: A burned ponderosa pine soil took up 49% more methane than unburned soil 10 years after fire, mostly because the organic layer was lost. A Swedish chronosequence ties uptake to humus depth. Fire can raise, lower or leave the sink unchanged depending on the ecosystem.

links.label: Methane sink along a fire chronosequence

why: Already studied, with mixed results.

untested: Whether beaver ponds lower downstream dissolved silica through diatom uptake and burial of biogenic silica. No study measured diatoms or burial in beaver ponds, or how the effect scales with how long the water stays in the pond.

papers.title: Correll et al. 2000: one pond, a 32% cut in dissolved silicate export (abstract only)
Sethna et al. 2025: an Indiana reservoir kept 49-58% of dissolved silica, but only about 30% of that was buried biogenic silica
Maavara et al. 2014: reservoirs and silica retention (abstract only)

web.text: Ponds and reservoirs do hold back dissolved silica, but the beaver-pond case is thin: one pond study and reservoir studies. A 2026 paper may have found no difference between ponds and upstream reaches (seen only as a search snippet), and a German pond reportedly released silica in summer.

why: Easy to test and plausible, but a first beaver-pond result already exists, so it is less new than it looks and the effect could reverse in shallow ponds.

untested: Whether soil right next to tree trunks takes up less methane than soil 1-2 m away because of stemflow wetting. No paper compares near-stem and between-tree soil for methane. One older beech and spruce study may show the opposite sign (seen only as a search snippet).

papers.title: Van Stan and Gordon 2018: review of stemflow and near-stem soils, with no methane data
Borken et al. 2006: excluding throughfall raised methane uptake, with a hump-shaped response to soil moisture
Fest et al. 2017: soil methane uptake (truncated abstract only)

web.text: Methane uptake responds to soil moisture in a hump-shaped way, so wetting near trunks could lower or raise it. Nothing found compares near-stem soil with soil between trees.

why: Looks new and is simple to measure, but the direction is the main risk: wetting could cut methane uptake or help it.

untested: Whether dust-derived phosphorus in surface soil is higher under tree crowns than in gaps. The canopy pathway is being studied, but not this field comparison.

papers.title: Gross et al. 2026 (preprint): foliar uptake and the canopy pathway in a Puerto Rican forest (abstract only)

web.text: Canopy interception and foliar uptake of dust phosphorus are being studied, so the idea is not far from active work. The soil-under-crown versus gap comparison was not found.

why: Testable, but the canopy route for dust phosphorus is already being studied, and foliar uptake could remove the effect in the soil.

untested: Whether sulfate reduction in waterlogged soils lowers bioavailable molybdate enough to make free-living nitrogen fixation molybdenum-limited, with a sulfate-by-molybdenum interaction. The nearest work is in plankton and seawater, not wet soils.

papers.title: Howarth and Cole 1985: sulfate inhibits molybdate uptake and nitrogen fixation in plankton and seawater (abstract only)

web.text: The sulfate and molybdenum link is established in seawater and plankton. The soil and wetland version was not confirmed, and the top keyword hits were off-topic.

why: A known marine mechanism carried into wet soils: plausible and testable with a simple sulfate-by-molybdenum experiment, but the idea is not far from existing work.

untested: Whether regional ice loss raises eruption rate and volcanic CO2 by about 2-6 times within 1-3 thousand years, and whether rapid modern melt gives a smaller lagged rise. Deglaciation and volcanism is already a studied link.

papers.title: Huybers and Langmuir 2009: feedback between deglaciation, volcanism and atmospheric CO2 (abstract only)

web.text: The link between ice loss and more volcanism is already proposed and studied for the last deglaciation. The size of the response and the modern lagged rise are the untested parts.

why: A real mechanism with a testable record, but the core idea has already been published, so it is mostly a refinement.

untested: Whether Southern Ocean productivity downstream of fast-spreading ridge plumes is higher than in matched waters with the same dust input.

papers.title: Tagliabue et al. 2010: hydrothermal iron and the Southern Ocean (abstract via a repository record)

web.text: Hydrothermal vents are known to supply iron to the Southern Ocean, and 476 papers mention both topics. The matched dust-versus-plume productivity comparison was not found.

why: Vent iron reaching the Southern Ocean is already studied; only the specific productivity comparison looks open.

untested: Whether coasts with high submarine groundwater discharge have more phytoplankton, scaling with the radium-derived discharge rate.

papers.title: Moore 2008: submarine groundwater discharge as a nutrient and chemical source to the coast (record via a repository)
Cho et al. 2018: groundwater discharge and coastal productivity

web.text: Groundwater is a known coastal nutrient source, and radium is the standard tracer. A broad comparison of phytoplankton against discharge rate across coasts was not found.

why: Very testable and plausible, but groundwater as a coastal nutrient source is well known, so the new part is small.

untested: Whether freezing soil speeds the chemical loss of nitrite and the production of nitric and nitrous oxide. Freeze-concentration raises nitrite reaction rates by a large factor in freezing solutions, but no one has measured it in soil, and one study found nitrite piling up in live soil at -2 C.

papers.title: Buessecker et al. 2019: chemical nitrous oxide production from nitrite in tropical peat (no freezing, one soil, no nitric oxide)
Green et al. 2022: nitrous oxide sources in soil (did not separate chemical from biological production or test subzero temperatures)

web.text: Takenaka et al. (1992, 1996) found nitrite reactions run about 100,000 times faster in freezing solutions at pH 4.5. No soil measurement was found, and Wertz et al. 2018 saw nitrite accumulate at -2 C in live soil, which argues against fast net loss. Soil buffering and the eutectic cut-off make the direction uncertain.

why: A strong mechanism in the lab that nobody seems to have tested in soil, and a clean experiment can settle it, but the one soil result points the other way.

untested: Whether fog formed on more aerosol (more, smaller droplets) delivers less water to the forest floor per hour of fog at the same liquid water content, because canopy capture falls steeply with droplet size. No study varied aerosol or droplet number and measured forest fog capture.

papers.title: Beswick et al. 1991: eddy-correlation over a forest; deposition rises with droplet size (did not vary aerosol)
Gallagher et al. 1992: size-resolved cloudwater deposition to forest and moorland (no clean versus polluted comparison)
Ding et al. 2026: large-eddy simulation of aerosol and fog (no vegetation capture, no water reaching the ground)

web.text: Capture by forest canopies is known to rise with droplet size, and aerosol is known to make fog droplets smaller and more numerous. Nothing found links the two to the water that reaches the ground. Atmospheric journals are poorly indexed in the paper search, so the counts understate what exists.

why: Combines two well-measured effects nobody seems to have joined, but aerosol also raises liquid water and fog duration, so the net sign for water delivered is uncertain.

untested: Whether raising sulfate in iron-poor wetland or paddy soils raises the share of nitrous oxide among denitrification products, and whether adding copper reverses it. The copper rescue has only been shown in pure cultures and bioreactors.

papers.title: A paper on nitrous oxide reduction in sulfidic waters: found no copper sulfide precipitate and did not add copper (read through a summary, not in full)
A paper on the copper chaperone for nitrous oxide reductase: below 0.5 uM copper a mutant strain accumulated up to about 4 mM nitrous oxide (read through a summary, not in full)
A paper describing the copper-sulfur cluster at the nitrous oxide reductase active site (read through a summary, not in full)

web.text: The enzyme that removes nitrous oxide needs copper, and sulfide can tie up copper in the lab. Only 1 paper mentions copper, sulfide and nitrous oxide together in wetlands or soils. Iron in porewater may keep sulfide too low to matter, and sulfide may poison the enzyme directly.

why: A clean, testable sulfate-by-copper experiment on a real enzyme mechanism, but the author checked the sources only through summaries and iron in porewater could remove the effect.

untested: Whether coastal catchments downwind of a strong marine heatwave export about 15-40% more river organic carbon per extreme-rain event than matched events without one. The heatwave-rain link and the storm-carbon link are each studied; no one has joined them.

papers.title: Wang et al. 2026: marine heatwaves make downwind extreme coastal rain 20-30% heavier, peaking 1-2 days later (nothing on rivers or carbon)
Renkl et al. 2026: a modelled heatwave-intensified atmospheric river with 19-55% more California rain (one event, no runoff or carbon)
Clark et al. 2022: extreme rainstorms drive exceptional organic carbon export from Puerto Rico rivers (summary page read)
Lee et al. 2017 (preprint): typhoons gave up to 25% of annual dissolved organic carbon flux in about 3% of the time in Taiwanese rivers

web.text: Heatwaves are shown to make coastal storms wetter, and big storms are shown to carry most of a river's carbon. Only 4 papers mention heatwaves, storms and organic carbon export together, and they are reviews that do not test this link. Extra rain may not mean extra carbon per millimetre.

why: Two well-documented effects nobody has joined, with data that already exist, but heavier rain may not carry more carbon per millimetre and the heatwave result comes from a single study.

untested: Whether poor pollination in pollinator-dependent crops (oilseed rape, sunflower, orchard fruit) leaves more nitrogen in the field and raises winter nitrate leaching. No paper measured seed nitrogen, soil nitrogen or leaching while varying pollination.

papers.title: Tamburini et al. 2017: sunflower, pollination and nitrogen (read in full; measured yield only, no seed nitrogen, soil nitrogen or leaching)
Bommarco et al. 2012: oilseed rape and pollination, +18% seed weight per plant (repository page; yield and quality only)
Marini et al. 2015: pollination and nitrogen interaction (abstract only)
Sieling and Kage 2006: only 13-25% of nitrogen surplus leaches (abstract only)
Bingham and Garzon 2023: in barley, late nitrogen uptake is limited by root supply, not grain demand (abstract only; counter-evidence)

web.text: Less seed means less nitrogen leaving in the harvest, which is close to certain by mass balance. Only 13-25% of extra surplus leaches, and crops may take up more nitrogen in leaves and stems, so the leaching signal could be 2-5 kg N per hectare and hard to detect. Only 5 papers mention pollination with nitrogen leaching, and none are on point by title.

why: A link between farm ecology and the nitrogen cycle that nobody seems to have measured, with a clear field design, but the leaching effect is small and crops can compensate.

untested: Whether soils and wetland sediments on copper-rich bedrock (such as basalt) release less nitrous oxide per unit of nitrate denitrified than soils on copper-poor bedrock (granite, quartz sandstone). Copper is known to matter to the enzyme that removes nitrous oxide, but the natural bedrock range has not been tested, and bedrock also changes pH and carbon.

papers.title: A wetland sediment study: 26 uM copper cut cumulative nitrous oxide to about 4-14% of added nitrate, versus 55-94% without copper
A study of the nitrous oxide reductase gene in Pseudomonas stutzeri: its transcription fell above 0.5 mM copper
A basalt-soil study: soils average 43.9 mg/kg copper, attributed to the basalt parent material

web.text: Copper is established as a requirement of the enzyme that turns nitrous oxide into nitrogen, and basalt soils are copper-rich. No paper combines bedrock copper, soil and the nitrous oxide ratio. A 2025 preprint (abstract only) links bedrock type to river nitrous oxide, so the geology link is already being studied. Bedrock also changes pH and carbon, which could swamp a copper effect.

why: A clean field comparison built on a proven enzyme mechanism, but bedrock changes several things at once and the copper doses tested so far were additions, not natural levels.

untested: Whether sulfide lowers dissolved nickel and cobalt in sulfate-amended, mineral-poor peat enough that part of the known sulfate suppression of wetland methane is a metal limitation of methanogens, not only competition. No paper combines sulfate, nickel or cobalt, and methane production in peat.

papers.title: Glass and Orphan 2012: trace metal requirements for the enzymes that make and consume methane and nitrous oxide (abstract; the first third of the paper read)
Gauci et al. 2004: sulfur pollution suppresses the wetland methane source (opening of the abstract only)
A 2019 paper on nickel and cobalt, methane production and methanogens in paddy soil (read in full; metal additions changed methane by only about 3-6%)

web.text: Sulfate is known to suppress wetland methane, and methanogens need nickel and cobalt. No paper combines the three: 30 papers cover sulfate and methane in peat, 3 cover nickel or cobalt and methane, and none cover both. Counter-evidence: metal additions raised methane only in mineral-poor peat, and changed it by only about 3-6% in paddy soil.

why: A clean 2x2 sulfate by nickel and cobalt incubation, but the general idea of trace-metal limits on methanogens is already stated and metal effects have been small in the one soil tested.

untested: The urban-to-rural NOx/ozone gradient scaling and the isotope-tracer partition under ozone alone (without elevated CO2) are untested; the core ozone effect was seen only transiently in the aspen FACE.

papers.title: Aspen FACE: with ambient O3 and CO2 both raised 50%, formation of total and acid-insoluble soil C fell ~50% relative to CO2 alone; did not test ozone alone, NOx gradients or long-term persistence
11-year follow-up at the same FACE: no significant main effect of O3 or CO2 on soil C; the early O3 reduction in new soil C proved temporary, mirroring fine-root biomass; no urban gradient

web.text: Loya et al. found roughly the predicted halving of new soil carbon, but only under elevated CO2 plus O3, and the later 11-year dataset from the same experiment showed the effect faded. The NOx-downwind scaling has not been tested.

why: Strength: a direct FACE precedent exists and the experiment is clear; risk: the same experiment found the effect was temporary, and the NOx scaling is an untested add-on.

untested: Site-level multi-year chamber records along a rainfall gradient regressed on lagged ENSO with soil water as mediator have not been done; the wet-forest sign (less waterlogging raises respiration) is untested and competes with a warming/drought-suppression effect in the wet tropics.

papers.title: Synthesis of East Asian forest soil respiration vs ENSO: positive correlation in tropical-subtropical zones, negative in warm temperate, mediated by monsoon precipitation anomalies; lags of months; database synthesis, not automated chambers or mediation by soil water

Tropical water availability versus CO2 growth-rate coupling became more negative 1989-2018, linked to ENSO teleconnection shifts; used atmospheric CO2 and water storage, did not measure soil respiration or a wet versus dry sign split

web.text: Regional syntheses show ENSO-linked soil respiration responses whose sign depends on climate zone and precipitation anomalies, matching the idea of a wetness-dependent sign. The specific waterlogging mechanism in wet forests is mostly inferred, and tropical El Nino heat and drought usually suppress carbon uptake rather than waterlogging.

links.label: ENSO and forest soil respiration, East Asia 2025

why: Strength: zone-dependent sign already shows up in synthesis data; risk: in wet forests El Nino warmth and drought usually dominate, so the waterlogging-relief sign may not hold.

untested: Upscaling to land-surface energy balance and evaporation using crust-cover maps and a land-surface model, and a scraped-versus-intact paired transect across a full successional gradient, are not yet done.

papers.title: Mature scytonemin-rich cyanobacterial biocrust raised surface soil temperature by up to 10 C and lowered albedo; plot scale, did not upscale to energy balance or evaporation

20-year warming experiment: crust shift to lightly pigmented cyanobacteria raised brightness 14% and changed surface temperature ~0.3 C per 10% cover; remote sensing at plot scale, argued the feedback is missing from process models
Warming and altered watering raised dryland biocrust albedo by more than 30% via crust community shifts; field experiment, no energy-balance modelling

web.text: The plot-scale effect (scytonemin crust darkens soil and warms it by several degrees, up to 10 C) is published, and follow-up work shows crust community shifts change albedo and temperature. The global-scale energy-balance and evaporation consequence is flagged as missing from models and remains the open part.

why: Strength: direct plot-scale measurements already support mechanism and sign; risk: upscaling to about 20% of land is uncertain because crust maps and mixed-pixel effects are weak.

untested: No study found adding Bdellovibrio or Myxococcus to AOB cultures or ammonium-amended soil and tracking amoA and nitrite; whether AOB flocs protect them from predators, and any ammonium dependence, is untested.

papers.title: Protozoan predation on AOB and anammox in nitritation-anammox biofilms by FISH-CLSM; showed predation of AOB occurs, but by amoebae, not predatory bacteria, and no nitrification rates
Review of Bdellovibrio-and-like organisms as biocontrol agents: prey range is broad Gram-negative bacteria; no data on nitrifier prey or nitrification effects

web.text: Predation on AOB is documented for protozoa and phages, and BALOs have broad Gram-negative prey ranges, so the mechanism is plausible. I found no direct test on nitrifiers, and aggregated, slow-growing nitrifier flocs may be poorly accessible to predators.

why: Strength: a simple culture experiment would settle it; risk: AOB live in protective aggregates and grow slowly, so predation may be too small to affect nitrification, and the high-ammonium claim is speculative.

untested: A controlled phage-enriched versus virus-reduced microcosm design with 18O-water CUE and amino-sugar markers is not found; existing results show the sign of the viral effect on CUE depends on soil fertility, opposite to the stated prediction in rich soils.

papers.title: Virus particle addition to agricultural soils raised microbial CUE and necromass by 14% in organically fertilized soil, but raised CO2 by 41% in unfertilized soil; contradicts the prediction in rich soils, supports it in poor soils
Long-term microplastic field experiment: viral lysis and virus-host coadaptation altered CUE and SOC accrual; correlative, not a manipulated virus-reduced design

web.text: Recent work directly manipulates soil viruses and finds both effects: virus addition boosted CUE and necromass in nutrient-rich soils but raised respiration in poor soils. The prediction of uniformly lower CUE with lysis is therefore too simple.

why: Strength: highly testable and already attempted; risk: published microcosms show virus addition can raise CUE and necromass, so direction depends on fertility.

untested: A controlled spectral measurement of paired soils along an organic carbon gradient at fixed moisture, with albedo forcing compared directly to CO2 forcing from the carbon change across soil types and climates, is not found; existing work is cropland modelling or two-site field trials.

papers.title: European cover-crop modelling with a soil darkening feedback scenario: higher SOC darkens soil and could erase ~20% of the climate benefit; model-based, not measured spectral albedo along a SOC gradient

Zimbabwe maize trials (EGU abstract): albedo forcing and SOC forcing were similar in size and opposite in sign on light sandy soil with mulch, but cooling on dark clay; two sites, two seasons, conference abstract

web.text: Soil darkening with organic matter is long known and recent studies quantify albedo forcing against SOC forcing, finding offsets from about 20% in Europe-wide modelling up to near-total offset on light sandy soil. The result depends strongly on soil type, snow and cover, so a general offset is not established.

why: Strength: mechanism and sign are supported by field and modelling work and the lab test is easy; risk: bare-soil albedo is rarely the exposed surface in real land use, so real-world offset is soil- and cover-dependent.

untested: Global or multi-biome test of sign by soil moisture regime using SRDB or flux towers with ENSO lags, and its contribution to CO2 growth-rate variability, is not done; most evidence is regional or atmospheric.

papers.title: Synthesis of East Asian forest soil respiration vs ENSO: sign differs between tropical-subtropical (positive) and warm temperate (negative) zones, heterotrophic more sensitive, driven by monsoon precipitation; regional only
Tropical water availability coupling to atmospheric CO2 growth rate, ENSO teleconnections; showed water control of the growth rate but did not separate soil respiration from photosynthesis

web.text: ENSO is known to drive interannual CO2 growth variability and a regional soil respiration synthesis finds opposite-sign responses by zone. Attribution of the growth-rate signal to soil respiration versus gross primary production and fire is unresolved.

links.label: ENSO and forest soil respiration, East Asia 2025

why: Strength: sign-by-regime logic matches existing regional data and is testable with existing databases; risk: soil respiration is hard to isolate from photosynthesis and fire in the CO2 growth rate.

untested: No study found that separates transpiration-driven drying from other plant effects on gross nitrification (planted versus unplanted or shaded pots at controlled evaporative demand with 15N pool dilution and amoA); plant ammonium uptake and nitrification-inhibitor exudates are confounding mechanisms.

papers.title: Planted versus unplanted forest soil under constant moisture or drying-rewetting: plant ammonium uptake halved by drying while microbial uptake rose; short 24 h assay, nitrification not measured

Shrubland soil incubation with 15N pool dilution across moisture and temperature: gross nitrification rose with water content and ceased below ~60% WHC; unplanted soil, no plant or transpiration effect

web.text: Nitrification is well known to depend on soil moisture with a mid-range optimum, and plants compete with nitrifiers for ammonium. Whether transpiration demand sets a moisture-driven nitrification peak, distinct from direct ammonium competition, has not been tested.

why: Strength: moisture dependence of nitrification is solid and an experiment is simple; risk: plant ammonium uptake, root exudates and biological nitrification inhibition can swamp any water effect.

untested: No field thaw-depth warming experiment with faunal exclusion (mesh bags or heat extraction) measuring CO2, CH4 and litter mass loss was found; the depth-range expansion of fauna into thawed layers and the effect beyond temperature alone are untested.

papers.title: Lab incubation of Yedoma permafrost with the springtail Folsomia candida for 25 days: CO2 rose ~26%, about half from springtail respiration and ~13% attributed to priming; single species, bacteria only, no field or depth test
Five years of open-top-chamber warming in permafrost wetlands (Great Hing'an Mountains): Collembola richness and abundance rose, about eightfold in April; no decomposition or carbon flux measured
Mini-review of arthropod responses to Arctic cryosphere decline including permafrost depth; highlights data gaps on functional roles

web.text: Warming increases springtail abundance in permafrost wetlands, and adding springtails to permafrost raised CO2 beyond their own respiration in the lab. What is missing is a field test with faunal exclusion that shows the effect on thawed-carbon loss and depth colonization.

why: Strength: lab priming and field abundance results both point the predicted way; risk: springtails are surface dwellers and may not reach deep thawed carbon, and fauna effects may be small relative to microbial thaw responses.

untested: Isotope tracing (33P or 15N) of nutrient delivery through hyphae to plants across snow-manipulation plots, and the generality beyond one subalpine meadow and AMF, are not shown; the preprint infers nutrient effects from soil pools. It also is not peer reviewed.

papers.title: Preprint: experimentally advanced snowmelt in a subalpine meadow caused plant greening to start early and cut extraradical AM hyphal production, with smaller available N and P pools; one site, not yet peer reviewed, nutrient transfer not traced

Hubbard Brook 29-month root-exclusion and ingrowth cores along a snow-depth gradient: grouped AM and EM abundance unaffected by snow depth, ericoid fungi rose with snow, some orders responded; single sampling, no hyphal timing or nutrient transfer

web.text: A recent early-snowmelt experiment reports plant-fungal asynchrony with reduced hyphal production and smaller nutrient pools, which closely matches the prediction. A forest snowpack-decline study found little change in grouped mycorrhizal abundance, so the effect may vary by system and fungal group.

why: Strength: a direct early-snowmelt experiment already shows the predicted mismatch; risk: forest and Arctic snow studies show mixed fungal responses and nutrient delivery has not been traced.

untested: Multi-year (3-5 year) persistence of the abundance-up, richness-down shift and its link to measured C and N turnover (CUE, N mineralisation) has not been shown; follow-ups were 7 months or less, and the copiotroph shift was inferred from taxa rather than traits or rates.

papers.title: Hurricane Otto, Costa Rica: soil sampled 3 months before and 7 months after; microbial biomass up, genus richness down, shift to dominant functional-group genera; single storm, short horizon, no turnover rates

Luquillo Canopy Trimming Experiment: green debris deposition and canopy opening decoupled; soil microbial community changed pre vs post but did not separate by treatment, effects possibly missed or masked; bacterial richness showed a positive response to some treatment

web.text: A Costa Rica study found the predicted abundance increase and richness decrease after a hurricane, but the best controlled experiment (Luquillo canopy trimming) found treatment effects were masked by strong background variation and resilience. Multi-year persistence and process-rate consequences remain unmeasured.

why: Strength: an observational precedent and an existing manipulation platform make it testable; risk: experimental work shows microbial resilience, so lasting copiotroph shifts and rate changes are uncertain.

untested: No test with trees in seasonally dry forest or shrubland that measures protease activity and gross N mineralization with lift blocked by trenching or shading and deuterium-labelled deep water; existing work is sagebrush with augmented deep water and grass in pots, with no protease assays.

papers.title: Sagebrush field experiment: adding deep water raised lift, soil respiration and 15N cycling in surface soil and N uptake into inflorescences; shrub not tree, no protease assay or blocked-lift control
Grass in two-layer pots with lift blocked by 24 h light: decomposition and uptake higher with lift, mixed NH4/NO3 signs; greenhouse, grass, no protease or gross mineralization by pool dilution
Hydraulic redistribution may stimulate decomposition: diel drying-rewetting of root litter in a desert system; decomposition only, not enzymes or N rates

web.text: Field and pot experiments show hydraulic lift raises topsoil decomposition and N cycling in sagebrush and grass. The specific claim for trees, protease activity and gross mineralization with a blocked-lift contrast, and the 20-100% size, are untested.

links.label: Hydraulic lift and N cycling in grass, 2012

why: Strength: a sagebrush field study already shows more surface N cycling with lift; risk: trenching and root exclusion confound lift with root death and competition, and lift in trees may be too small to matter.

untested: A clean forested-versus-sparse basin contrast of runoff ratio against CO2 with precipitation, temperature, land use and leaf area as covariates, backed by FACE sap-flow checks, is not settled; the global catchment attribution found near-zero median CO2 effect, so the predicted runoff-ratio rise is not detected.

papers.title: Global climate model with a vegetation component: physiological forcing from doubled CO2 raised simulated global runoff by about 6%; a model projection, not an observed basin trend

Catchment-scale attribution across 1116 unimpacted catchments, 1981-2020, constrained by observed streamflow: median direct CO2 contribution approached zero; the opposite of a detectable decades-long runoff-ratio rise

web.text: Models predict higher runoff from CO2-driven stomatal closure, but observation-constrained catchment analyses find the net effect is close to zero because greater leaf area and growth offset the lower conductance. Other work argues the effect depends on aridity, so the sign can differ by climate.

links.label: Direct CO2 effect on streamflow, Nat Commun 2024

why: Strength: well-defined regression and strong mechanistic basis; risk: observation-based attribution already finds a near-zero effect, with leaf-area greening and climate offsets cancelling stomatal closure.

untested: The size and persistence of the effect for atmospheric deposition specifically (as opposed to fertilizer additions) at chronic low doses, and in which soils the response saturates or declines, are less clear; the core N-raises-phosphatase link is already established.

papers.title: Meta-analysis of 34 studies: N fertilization enhanced phosphatase activity from tropics to extra-tropics, in roots and bulk soil, while P fertilization suppressed it; mostly fertilizer, not deposition gradients
Letter on long-term N addition: N stimulation of soil phosphatase appears to decline progressively with years of N addition, citing a long-term chaparral-type record; indicates the effect can fade
7-year simulated N deposition in calcareous grassland raised root-surface phosphomonoesterase activity in three plant functional types; plant roots not bulk soil

web.text: A multi-biome meta-analysis finds N addition raises phosphatase activity, and deposition-simulation experiments show the same in plant roots. Evidence that the stimulation can fade with decades of N addition means the direction holds but the long-term size is uncertain.

links.label: Deposition and root phosphatase, calcareous grassland

why: Strength: a meta-analysis across biomes already shows the predicted direction; risk: little novelty, and long-term N saturation can erase the effect.

untested: Validation against deep hydrographic sections and abyssal temperature trends with modern flux maps and eddy-resolving or multi-model comparisons is incomplete; existing numbers come from one global model configuration and the Arctic deep-warming signal exceeds what geothermal heating explains.

papers.title: Ocean model with no, uniform and spatially varying geothermal heat flux: with strong mixing the AABW cell strengthened about 15% (2.5 Sv), deep North Pacific warmed up to 0.3 C and Southern Ocean poleward heat transport rose about 10%; single model, climatological data

Deep Arctic Ocean warming observed at 0.020 C/decade exceeds what geothermal heating explains; attributes the excess to heat transferred from the deep Atlantic; does not test global overturning with and without geothermal flux
Coupled climate model preprint: geothermal heating weakens deep stratification and strengthens AABW and deepens the AMOC in the Last Glacial Maximum, with a different sea-ice response today; preprint

web.text: Emile-Geay and Madec ran ocean model pairs with and without spatially varying geothermal heat flux and reported about a 15% stronger AABW cell and about 10% more Southern Ocean poleward heat transport, almost exactly the stated estimate. What remains is observational validation and robustness across models.

why: Strength: the stated 10-15% AABW and heat-transport estimates match a published model result; risk: results depend on the mixing parameterization, and little new remains beyond observational validation.

untested: No study found pairing debris-rich and debris-poor glacier catchments and linking dust grain size and mineralogy to the weathering or erosion rate of surrounding rock; existing work shows dust and local moraine sources matter at single glaciers but does not test the weathering-rate dependence or the 1-9 W/m2 range.

papers.title: Vadret da Morteratsch: summer albedo fell 0.32 to 0.15 after 2003 from mineral and biogenic dust, ~3.5 m extra ice loss over 2003-06 (equal to +1.7 K air temperature); moraine dust named as an important feedback; one glacier, no weathering-rate link
Argentiere Glacier model: Saharan dust cut annual mass balance by 0.31-0.45 m w.e. and accounted for about 8-16% of summer melt; long-range dust, modelled, no catchment debris or weathering analysis

web.text: Dust on glaciers, including dust from exposed moraines and bedrock, lowers albedo and speeds melt, with effects ranging from small to large by site and a tropical Andes study finding under 1% reflectivity loss. The specific dependence on weathering intensity of the surrounding catchment is not tested.

why: Strength: dust-darkening of glaciers is documented, including from local moraines; risk: dust amount depends on wind, source exposure and snow cover more than on weathering rate, so the proposed causal link may be weak or confounded.

untested: No study found regressing dust immersion-freezing temperature against a weathering index (such as CIA) with measured feldspar content; existing work characterises pure feldspars and shows feldspar dominates dust ice nucleation, not how source-soil weathering changes it. Biological and organic ice nucleators in soil dust can mask feldspar at warmer temperatures.

papers.title: Droplet-freezing assays: feldspar, especially K-feldspar, dominates ice nucleation by mineral dust at mixed-phase conditions despite being a minor component, clays unimportant; did not vary source weathering intensity

Survey of 15 feldspars: K-rich alkali feldspars usually nucleate ice better than Ca-bearing plagioclase, large within-group variability, some activity loss when aged in water (about 2 C for hyper-active K-feldspar over 16 months); pure minerals, not weathered soil dusts
Perthite feldspar powders: onset -2 to -4 C and site populations tied to exsolution and microcline structure; industrial powders, no weathering gradient

web.text: Feldspar content and structure control mineral-dust ice nucleation, and ageing in water lowers activity somewhat, so weathering that removes K-feldspar should reduce activity. I found no measurement along a weathering-intensity gradient, and the size of a few degrees C shift is untested.

why: Strength: a clean field-to-lab gradient test with XRD and freezing assays; risk: soil dust also carries organic and biological ice nucleators, and clays or surface coatings could shift activity independently of feldspar content.

untested: Direct 14C-dead CO2 measurements in soil gas and river water along an erosion-rate gradient on shale, with microbial-inhibitor incubations, are only partly done; the heat released by rock organic carbon respiration is not measured or shown to matter.

papers.title: Taiwan Central Range soils: on average 67% of bedrock OCpetro oxidised in soils, CO2 emission 6.1-18.6 t C/km2/yr rising with erosion rate; microbial mediation shown by lipid biomarkers and isotopes; did not use inhibitors or measure heat

Rhenium-based global catchment extrapolation: rock organic carbon oxidation releases CO2 rivalling or exceeding silicate weathering drawdown, hotspots in uplifted fine-grained sedimentary mountains; flux estimate from rhenium, not direct respiration

web.text: Rhenium and biomarker work shows rock organic carbon is oxidised in soils and rivers with fluxes that rise with erosion rate, and that oxidation is microbially mediated. The global flux estimate and Taiwan share match the stated figures in kind, while respiration heat and inhibitor-controlled incubations are not reported.

why: Strength: the erosion-rate dependence and microbial mediation are published and the proposed test is established practice; risk: the heat-release claim is trivial and unmeasurable in practice, and the CO2 flux has chemical (abiotic) oxidation as a competing pathway.

untested: A matched-hillslope comparison with different weathering depth and fracture density at equal rainfall, scaling dry-season transpiration share (the 10-30% of annual rainfall estimate) with fracture density and weathering depth, is not found; existing work shows bedrock water use is widespread but not how it scales across sites.

papers.title: Continental-US estimate of bedrock-water contribution to transpiration: woody plants routinely access rock moisture, not only in drought; lower-bound estimate from datasets, no matched-hillslope or fracture-density scaling
Direct observation of rock moisture in a weathered-bedrock hillslope: weathered zone tens of metres thick stores water that plants draw down; one site, no cross-site comparison with unfractured rock
Review of bedrock as a tree water reservoir under drought: notes uncertainty on pathways and efficiency of rock-root exchange; synthesis not a matched test

web.text: Several studies show trees draw on water stored in weathered or fractured bedrock, especially in dry seasons, and that this is widespread. The dose-response with fracture density and the specific transpiration share are not established.

why: Strength: bedrock water use by trees is well documented and the proposed measurements are established; risk: confounding by rooting depth, species and climate makes a clean matched-site contrast hard, and thick weathered rock can also lower runoff rather than raise transpiration.
